Classic dispensationalism teaches that the rapture is imminent and that no prophesied event must come before it. The prophetic "clock" for Israel is said to be stopped. If that is so, then news events cannot show how close the rapture is, and believers will not be on earth for Armageddon anyway. Yet much popular writing reasons this way: Armageddon looks near, so the rapture must be nearer. One prominent seminary leader was described in 1991 as convinced that recent events had met the prophecies on the "Armageddon calendar". On the fulfilled reading, this shows a gap between the system's theory and its practice. It turns a doctrine of "no signs" into an industry of signs. It also draws attention away from the time words Jesus actually gave (Matthew 24:34).
Christianity Today (29 April 1991) described the "Armageddon calendar" being updated during the Gulf War.
Pretribulational writers often say events "cast their shadows before them". They mean signs of the tribulation can be seen before the rapture.

Dispensationalists answer that they do not claim signs for the rapture. They say "stage-setting" for the tribulation, such as Israel's return and world alliances, is visible beforehand, and that the rapture comes before all of it. Many of them also warn against sensationalism and date-setting.
How can writers say we are "approaching Armageddon" while also saying no one knows when it will come?
The two claims pull against each other. If there are no time markers, no one can know it is near. And if "near" can mean two thousand years, the word has lost its meaning.

Some writers say that Armageddon is near and that "there are no specific time indicators". Others say plainly that they believe it is near without explaining why. On the fulfilled reading, this is the reverse of how the New Testament speaks. Jesus gave clear time markers: "this generation will not pass away" (Matthew 24:34), and "some standing here will not taste death" (Matthew 16:28). Revelation says its events must "soon take place" and "the time is near" (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:10). Futurism stretches these words across many centuries. Yet it uses "near" for its own forecasts. If "near" can mean two thousand years, then saying Armageddon is "near" today tells us nothing. The fulfilled reading takes the Bible's time words at face value and lets them define the event.
Revelation 22:10: "Do not seal up the words... for the time is near". Compare Daniel 12:4, 9, where the words are sealed because the time was far off.
Matthew 26:18: "My time is near". Jesus was crucified within days.

Futurists reply that "near" means the next great event on God's calendar, which can happen at any time. They also cite God's patience (2 Peter 3:8-9). Many futurist scholars openly criticise writers who claim Armageddon is close.
Should Christians fear a coming false world peace, or a coming world war?
Popular prophecy teaching warns about both: a deceptive global peace and an unavoidable war. The fulfilled reading says Christians should pursue peace and justice, not wait for either script.

Some writers warn that a world peace is coming soon and that it will be a trap set by Antichrist. They base this on "Peace and safety!" in 1 Thessalonians 5:3. Others say a final war is fixed and that peace efforts are useless. This leaves believers confused: should they oppose peace treaties or work against war? Often the answer offered is an escape by rapture before any choice must be made. On the fulfilled reading, 1 Thessalonians 5:3 described the false confidence of Jerusalem before its sudden destruction (compare Jeremiah 6:14). It is not a warning against every peace treaty today. Jesus blesses peacemakers (Matthew 5:9). Scripture calls believers to pray for rulers "that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life" (1 Timothy 2:2), and Isaiah foresaw nations beating swords into ploughshares under Messiah's rule (Isaiah 2:4).
Jeremiah 6:14: false prophets cried "Peace, peace" before Babylon came in 586 BC. This is the pattern behind 1 Thessalonians 5:3.
Josephus, Jewish War 6.5.2: false prophets promised rescue right up to the temple's burning.

Futurists hold that 1 Thessalonians 5:3 points to a final false peace, perhaps a treaty involving Israel (Daniel 9:27). They agree, though, that believers should still seek peace in daily life. Postmillennialists expect real, growing peace through the gospel before Christ returns.
Why do Armageddon predictions keep needing to be adjusted?
Because they tie Scripture to the news, and the news keeps changing. Dates such as AD 2000, or claims that a planned invasion was "cancelled", show how the scenario is reworked after each failure.

One popular author suggested that AD 2000 was a likely end date for the "last days". He even named a possible day in October 2000 for the kingdom to begin, while also saying God may speed up or delay the timing. Another writer, after the 1982 Lebanon war, claimed that a Soviet invasion of Israel had been planned and that it had been "cancelled" by Israel's action. These adjustments follow a pattern. When events do not happen as forecast, a new explanation is added rather than questioning the system. Scripture gives a clear test for prophets: if the word does not come to pass, it is not from the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:22). On the fulfilled reading, the safer path is to read prophecy by its own time markers. Then it does not need to be reset with each news cycle.
2000: the predicted end-time dates passed without the events forecast.
Dwight Wilson, Armageddon Now! (1977), traces how premillennial forecasts about Russia and Israel shifted after 1917.

Futurist scholars also reject date-setting and agree with this critique of sensational writers. But they hold that a real future battle stays taught in Scripture even when popularisers fail. They warn against judging a doctrine by its worst advocates.
How often does the Bible mention Armageddon, and do the Old Testament prophets describe it?
The word appears only once, in Revelation 16:16. No Old Testament prophet uses it. The idea of one final world war centred on Israel is built by combining many other texts.

"Har-Magedon" occurs only in Revelation 16:16. There the kings of the whole world are gathered "for the war of the great day of God, the Almighty" (16:14). Popular books sometimes say that "the prophets" described it as a final suicidal world war in the Middle East. But the term is absent from the Old Testament, and none of the prophets gives that picture under that name. The modern scenario comes from joining Ezekiel 38-39, Joel 3, Zechariah 12-14, Daniel 11 and Revelation 19 into one future event. On the fulfilled reading, each of those passages has its own setting and time. Merging them into one battle is a choice made by the system, not a statement of the text.
Revelation 16:16 is the single occurrence. Its Greek form is Harmagedon ("Armageddon" in the KJV).
Ezekiel 38-39 (Gog), Joel 3 (Jehoshaphat valley) and Zechariah 14 (Jerusalem) each name a different place.

Futurists answer that the event can be taught in many texts even if the name appears once. They say gathered nations, a battle at Jerusalem and the Lord's intervention form one consistent theme. Amillennialists often see Revelation 16, 19 and 20 as the same final conflict told three times.
Does "Armageddon" mean the mountain of Megiddo or the city of Megiddo?
Har-Magedon means "mountain of Megiddo", but Megiddo is a mound in a plain, with no great mountain. Some, such as Bengel, suggested "city (ar) of Megiddo". Either way, the name is symbolic.

John says the place is called Har-Magedon "in Hebrew" (Revelation 16:16). Har means mountain. But Megiddo was a city mound overlooking the Jezreel plain, and no mountain carries that name. So interpreters have long asked what John meant. J. A. Bengel (1742) and some others read ar, "city", giving "city of Megiddo". Others link it to nearby Mount Carmel, where Elijah defeated the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). Still others read Isaiah's "mount of assembly" (har moed, Isaiah 14:13). On the fulfilled reading, the name is a symbol of decisive covenant judgment drawn from Megiddo's history. It does not mark a literal map point. A "city" sense would fit the idea that the real battle fell on a city: Jerusalem.
Tel Megiddo stands about 60 metres above the Jezreel Valley. It is a mound of ancient cities, not a mountain.
1 Kings 18:19-40: Mount Carmel, near Megiddo, was the scene of God's judgment on Baal's prophets.

Futurists take Har-Magedon as the Jezreel Valley near Megiddo. They see it as the staging area for a final campaign that ends at Jerusalem. Many scholars from all schools see a symbolic place name, possibly echoing "mount of assembly" (Isaiah 14:13), for the gathering of rebels against God.
What battles happened at Megiddo, and which one does Revelation recall?
Deborah and Barak's victory (Judges 5:19) and King Josiah's death in 609 BC both happened there. On the fulfilled reading, Josiah's defeat best fits a judgment on Israel's own city.

Megiddo guarded the main pass between Egypt and Mesopotamia, so many armies fought there. Thutmose III won there about 1457 BC. Deborah and Barak defeated the Canaanite kings "at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo" (Judges 5:19). Ahaziah of Judah died there (2 Kings 9:27). King Josiah went out against Pharaoh Neco, though God had warned him through Neco himself. Josiah was mortally wounded at Megiddo in 609 BC (2 Kings 23:29; 2 Chronicles 35:20-24). After that, Judah declined quickly toward the exile. On the fulfilled reading, Megiddo stood for a decisive battle whose meaning depends on who is guilty. Revelation's focus on judgment against the "great city" suggests the Josiah pattern: Israel's own disaster.
2 Chronicles 35:22: Josiah "did not listen to the words of Neco from the mouth of God" and fought at Megiddo.
1918: General Allenby defeated Ottoman forces near Megiddo. He was later made Viscount Allenby of Megiddo.

Futurists stress the victory pattern of Judges 5. In their view God defeats the nations gathered against his people, as in Zechariah 14:3. Others see Megiddo as a general symbol of decisive battle, with no single Old Testament event in view.
Why is Josiah's death at Megiddo linked with mourning in Zechariah 12?
Judah mourned Josiah for generations. Zechariah uses "the mourning in the plain of Megiddo" as the standard of great grief, and John echoes the same chapter about mourning for the one they pierced.

2 Chronicles 35:24-25 says all Judah mourned for Josiah. Jeremiah wrote a lament, and singers still remembered him in the Chronicler's day. Zechariah 12:10-11 says that when they look on "him whom they pierced", the mourning in Jerusalem will be as great as "the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the plain of Megiddo". John applies the "pierced" words to Jesus' crucifixion (John 19:37) and to his coming with the clouds (Revelation 1:7). On the fulfilled reading, Megiddo in Revelation 16:16 carries this sorrow. Just as Megiddo marked Judah's turn toward exile, the "Megiddo" of Revelation marks Jerusalem's final grief when the city that pierced its Messiah was judged in AD 70.
Zechariah 12:11: "the mourning of Hadadrimmon in the valley of Megiddo".
Revelation 1:7: "every eye will see him, including those who pierced him... the tribes of the land will mourn".

Futurists read Zechariah 12 as Israel's national repentance when Christ returns in the future. They see the mourning as sorrow that leads to salvation, not judgment. Amillennialists often apply it to repentance through the gospel, starting at Pentecost (Acts 2:37).
How can a battle called "Megiddo" actually be about Jerusalem?
Revelation regularly gives places symbolic names. It calls Jerusalem "Sodom and Egypt" (11:8). In the same way, "Megiddo" names the kind of judgment, not the map location.

Revelation uses Old Testament names as symbols. A false teacher is "Jezebel" (2:20). The city "where their Lord was crucified" is "spiritually called Sodom and Egypt" (11:8). On the fulfilled reading, the "great city" judged in Revelation is also "Babylon" (14:8; 16:19). Jerusalem was not literally Sodom or Egypt. It had taken on their character. So "Har-Magedon" need not be a literal valley. It names the kind of battle: God's decisive defeat of a rebel people. Revelation 16:19 shows the result: "the great city was split into three parts". Josephus describes Jerusalem in AD 70 as divided among three warring factions under John, Simon and Eleazar (Jewish War 5.1.1-4).
Revelation 11:8: "the great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified".
Josephus, Jewish War 5.1.4: the city was split among three factions during the siege of AD 70.

Most futurists and many others identify Babylon with Rome or a future world system, not Jerusalem. They also see Armageddon as a real campaign in Israel. Idealists read every place name as a symbol of the world's enmity to God in every age.
Is there any historical link between Megiddo and the Roman campaign against Jerusalem?

Some link is possible. In AD 70 Titus gathered his forces at Caesarea, near Mount Carmel. Troops from the north would naturally come through the Jezreel corridor by Megiddo before marching on Jerusalem.

After Vespasian became emperor, he sent Titus to finish the war. Josephus says Titus marched from Alexandria to Caesarea and decided to gather all his forces there (Jewish War 4.11.5). Legions and allied troops came from Syria and beyond, including detachments from the Euphrates (5.1.6). Caesarea lies on the coast just south of Mount Carmel. Roads from Syria and Galilee crossed the Jezreel Valley by Megiddo. In spring AD 70 Titus marched on Jerusalem. On the fulfilled reading, this gives a fitting backdrop to "gathering" the kings at Har-Magedon. Still, the main point stays symbolic: whether the image is literal or figurative, the war it describes ended in AD 70.
Josephus, Jewish War 4.11.5 (4.658-663): Titus goes from Alexandria to Caesarea to muster his army.
Titus besieged Jerusalem with four legions: V, X, XII and XV (Jewish War 5.1.6; 5.2.3).

Critics reply that Titus's muster at Caesarea is a thin link. They note that Revelation 16 speaks of kings "of the whole world" from the east (16:12), crossing the Euphrates. Futurists see a future eastern army. Historicists have linked it to the Ottoman power.
How could Rome's attack on Jerusalem be the gathering of "the kings of the whole world"?
Rome ruled an "empire of nations" that the New Testament calls "the whole world" (Luke 2:1). Its armies included allied kings and troops from many peoples.

Luke says that Caesar's decree went out that "all the world" (oikoumene) should be registered (Luke 2:1). He meant the Roman world. Rome then ruled from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Syria, with perhaps 50 to 80 million people. Titus's army included four legions plus forces from client kings: Agrippa II, Sohaemus of Emesa, Antiochus of Commagene, and Arab allies (Tacitus, Histories 5.1). Revelation 16:14 speaks of "the kings of the whole world" gathered for war. On the fulfilled reading, the nations under Rome, and their kings, came against Jerusalem as Jesus foretold. The king "sent his armies, destroyed those murderers and burned their city" (Matthew 22:7).
Tacitus, Histories 5.1: allied kings and Arab troops joined Titus's legions in AD 70.
Acts 11:28: Agabus foresaw a famine "over all the world". It struck in Claudius's reign (about AD 46-48).

Futurists say "the whole world" in Revelation 16:14 is global, so it requires a future coalition of nations. Amillennialists see the world's final assault on the church (Revelation 20:8-9). Idealists see the ongoing conflict between the world and God's people.
What reasons does the fulfilled reading give for placing Armageddon in the first century?
Three reasons: Jesus placed the great tribulation within his generation, Revelation says its events were "near", and Jesus warned that judgment would fall on the city that rejected him.

First, Jesus said all the events of Matthew 24, including the great tribulation, would happen before "this generation" passed (Matthew 24:34). Second, Revelation repeatedly says its events "must soon take place" and that "the time is near" (Revelation 1:1, 3; 22:6, 10). It also says Christ is coming "quickly" (3:11; 22:7, 12, 20). Third, Jesus warned Jerusalem that its house would be left desolate. He wept that enemies would surround the city because it did not know the time of its visitation (Matthew 23:38; Luke 19:41-44). On the fulfilled reading, the battle of the great day of God was Rome's war on Jerusalem, AD 66-70. It is not a nuclear war still waiting to happen. Christians need not fear it as a future doom.
Luke 19:43-44: "your enemies will build an embankment around you". Titus built a siege wall around the city in AD 70 (Jewish War 5.12.2).
Revelation 22:10 tells John not to seal the book, "for the time is near".

Futurists say Revelation 16-19 describes worldwide, cosmic events. They point to the return of Christ on a white horse (Revelation 19:11-21), which they believe has not happened. Amillennialists place Armageddon at the end of history as the final defeat of evil.
Does "His blood be on us and on our children" (Matthew 27:25) place guilt on Jewish people in every age?

No. The cry belonged to one crowd at one moment. On the fulfilled reading, its consequence fell within that generation in AD 70. Scripture forbids blaming children for their parents' sins, and the apostles offered forgiveness to those very people.

Matthew records the crowd's cry before Pilate (Matthew 27:25). On the fulfilled reading, "our children" points to the generation that saw Jerusalem fall about forty years later. That matches Jesus' warning: "all these things will come upon this generation" (Matthew 23:36). Scripture teaches that the son does not bear the father's guilt (Ezekiel 18:20). Peter offered forgiveness to the very people who had called for the crucifixion (Acts 2:23, 36-38; 3:14-19), and thousands of them believed. Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). For centuries some Christians misused this verse to justify hatred and violence against Jewish people. That was a grave sin against Christ and against his people. Every reading must reject it.
1965: the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate stated that Jews of later times cannot be charged with Christ's death.
Acts 3:17: Peter says the people and their rulers acted "in ignorance", and calls them to repent.

Interpreters of all schools today reject collective, lasting guilt. Some scholars see Matthew 27:25 as a crowd's formula of legal responsibility. Others read it as an ironic hint that Jesus' blood brings forgiveness (Matthew 26:28). Futurists stress God's continuing love for Israel (Romans 11:28-29).
What events does dispensationalism place in a future seventieth week of Daniel?

It places a seven-year tribulation after the rapture. In it the Antichrist rises, makes and breaks a covenant with Israel, a rebuilt temple is defiled, judgments fall, 144,000 Israelites are sealed, and Armageddon is fought.

In the dispensational scheme, as Anthony Hoekema summarised it, the church is raptured before the final "week" of Daniel 9:27. Seven years then follow, and the last three and a half are the "great tribulation". The Antichrist rises and later demands worship. God's judgments of Revelation 6-19 fall on the earth. A "gospel of the kingdom" is preached. A remnant of Israel, the 144,000 of Revelation 7, turns to Christ. Through them a great multitude of Gentiles is saved. Finally the armies of the beast gather at Armageddon. The whole structure rests on one claim: that Daniel's seventieth week is separated from the first sixty-nine by the church age. On the fulfilled reading, if that gap is not in the text, the structure has no foundation.
Revelation 4:1 ("Come up here") is read by many dispensationalists as a picture of the rapture before the seven years.
Pretribulationists say the seven years make up Daniel's seventieth week, with Revelation 6-19 inside it.

Dispensationalists hold that this is the natural result of reading Daniel 9 and Revelation literally and in order. Prewrath and posttribulational futurists keep the future seventieth week but place the rapture later in it. Amillennialists and postmillennialists generally deny a future seven-year period.
Why does dispensationalism need a gap between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks?
Without the gap, there is no future seven-year tribulation, no pretribulational rapture and no rebuilt temple in that period. The fulfilled reading says the gap comes from the system, not the text.

Daniel 9:24 says "seventy weeks are decreed". The sixty-nine weeks run to "Messiah the Prince" (9:25-26), and most evangelical interpreters agree they reach the time of Christ. Dispensationalism teaches that when Israel rejected Jesus, God stopped Israel's prophetic clock. The clock will start again only after the rapture. So the seventieth week is placed in the future, after a church age now nearly two thousand years long. That is about four times as long as the whole 490 years. A. J. McClain called this prophecy the most crucial in prophetic study. On the fulfilled reading, nothing in Daniel 9:24-27 mentions a gap, a pause or a parenthesis. The gap is needed only to keep the rest of the system working.
490 years were decreed. The proposed gap is already about 1,990 years, roughly four times longer than the prophecy itself.
The gap idea grew in the 1800s through J. N. Darby and was spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909).

Dispensationalists answer that verse 26 lists events (Messiah cut off, city destroyed) "after" the sixty-two weeks, not inside the seventieth. So a break is implied. They also note that some early writers, such as Hippolytus (about AD 204), placed the last week at the end of the age.
How is the "gap" in Daniel 9 like other gaps that interpreters have added to Scripture?
The fulfilled reading compares it to the Genesis "gap theory" and to a supposed gap between the legs and toes of Daniel 2's statue. In each case, a gap is inserted to fit an outside system.

In the 1800s, the "gap theory" (or ruin-and-reconstruction theory) placed long geological ages between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2. It was popularised by the Scofield Reference Bible and was meant to harmonise Genesis with the geology of the time. Creation scholar Henry Morris later criticised it for having no basis in the text. Some dispensational writers similarly place a long gap between the iron legs and the toes of Nebuchadnezzar's statue (Daniel 2:40-43). One admitted that an extended gap "must be fixed" somewhere in the image so it can reach the millennium. Clarence Larkin's charts drew the toes stretched across two thousand years. On the fulfilled reading, the same method is at work in each case: the system decides where the text must have a gap.
Scofield Reference Bible (1909), note on Genesis 1:2: it presents the ruin-and-reconstruction gap as a possibility.
Daniel 2:44: God sets up his kingdom "in the days of those kings". The text names no gap.

Dispensationalists reply that the cases are not alike. They say Scripture plainly has prophetic gaps elsewhere. One example is Isaiah 61:1-2, where Jesus stopped reading before "the day of vengeance" (Luke 4:18-20). Many of them also reject the Genesis gap theory themselves.
When was the kingdom of Daniel 2 set up: in the first century or after a future gap?
Daniel says God sets up his kingdom "in the days of those kings", during the fourth empire, Rome. Jesus announced that the kingdom was at hand during Rome's rule.

Nebuchadnezzar's statue shows four kingdoms in sequence: gold, silver, bronze and iron. They are usually identified as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. A stone cut without hands strikes the statue and becomes a mountain filling the earth (Daniel 2:34-35, 44-45). Daniel says God will set up this kingdom "in the days of those kings". On the fulfilled reading, the kings are the four empires, especially the fourth. The toes are never called kings or kingdoms in the text. Jesus came while Rome ruled. He said, "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand" (Mark 1:15). He also said, "the kingdom of God has come upon you" (Matthew 12:28). So the stone-kingdom began in the first century. It has been growing like a mountain ever since, with no pause needed.
Mark 1:15: "the time is fulfilled". This points to a prophetic timetable reaching its goal.
Matthew 13:31-33: the kingdom grows like a mustard seed and leaven. This matches the stone that grows into a mountain.

Dispensationalists see the stone striking the feet and toes as Christ's second coming. In their view it destroys a future ten-nation confederacy, and then the millennial kingdom fills the earth. Amillennialists agree the kingdom began at Christ's first coming but expect its fullness at his return.
How does the 490-year calendar of Daniel 9 fit history without a gap?
One reckoning starts from Artaxerxes' decree to Ezra in 458 BC. 483 years reach AD 26, when Jesus' ministry began. He was "cut off" mid-week (about AD 30); the week ended about AD 33.

Daniel 9:25 counts from "the going out of the word to restore and build Jerusalem". J. Barton Payne and many older writers start with Artaxerxes I's decree to Ezra in his seventh year, 458/457 BC (Ezra 7:7-26). Ezra 9:9 speaks of God giving "a wall in Judah and Jerusalem". Sixty-nine weeks are 483 years. From 458 BC, and since there is no year zero, they reach AD 26. That is close to Jesus' baptism and anointing by the Spirit (Luke 3:21-23). In the middle of the seventieth week, about AD 30, the Messiah was "cut off" (Daniel 9:26) and ended the worth of the sacrifices. The remaining three and a half years brought the covenant first to Israel. Around AD 33-34 Stephen was martyred, Paul was converted and the gospel turned to the Gentiles.
458 BC + 483 years = AD 26 (no year 0). Luke 3:1 dates John's ministry to Tiberius's fifteenth year, about AD 28-29 on most counts, or AD 26-27 if counted from his co-regency.
Acts 10-11: Cornelius, the first Gentile convert, was received a few years after the cross.

Many dispensationalists start from Nehemiah's commission in 444 BC (Nehemiah 2:1-8). They use 360-day "prophetic years", as Sir Robert Anderson and Harold Hoehner did, and reach the triumphal entry about AD 32-33. Critical scholars apply the weeks to Antiochus IV and the crisis of 167-164 BC.
Who "makes a firm covenant with the many" in Daniel 9:27: the Messiah or the Antichrist?
On the fulfilled reading, the Messiah. Jesus spoke of "my blood of the covenant, poured out for many" (Matthew 26:28). Nothing in Daniel 9 mentions an Antichrist.

The nearest person in Daniel 9:26 is "Messiah", who is cut off. "The people of the prince who is to come" are the subject of the next clause, but "the prince" himself is not the main subject. Verse 27 then says "he will confirm a covenant with the many for one week" and "in the middle of the week he will cause the sacrifice and offering to cease". At the Last Supper Jesus said, "This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many" (Matthew 26:28). This uses both key words, "covenant" and "many" (compare Isaiah 53:11-12). Hebrews says Christ "takes away the first in order to establish the second" (Hebrews 10:9). On the fulfilled reading, the Messiah confirmed the covenant and ended the worth of sacrifice by his death. Philip Mauro and many older commentators read it this way.
Isaiah 53:11-12: the Servant "will justify many" and "bore the sin of many". This is the same "many" as in Daniel 9:27.
John 19:30: "It is finished". On this reading, the moment sacrifice lost its meaning before God.

Dispensationalists argue that the nearest antecedent of "he" is "the prince who is to come" (9:26). They hold that this ruler, from the Roman people who destroyed the temple, makes a seven-year treaty and breaks it. Many critical scholars see Antiochus IV, who stopped the sacrifices in 167 BC.
How could the Messiah "cause the sacrifice to cease" if the temple sacrifices continued until AD 70?

From God's covenant standpoint, Christ's death made the sacrifices obsolete: "It is finished." The rites went on for a time, but they had lost their purpose. Hebrews says the old covenant was "ready to vanish away".

Dispensationalists rightly note that priests kept offering sacrifices for about forty years after the cross. But Daniel 9:24 states the purpose of the weeks: "to finish transgression, to make an end of sins, to make atonement for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness". Christ did those things at the cross. At his death the temple veil tore from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51). Hebrews says that where sins are forgiven "there is no longer any offering for sin" (Hebrews 10:18). On the fulfilled reading, the sacrifices "ceased" in God's legal sense when the true sacrifice was offered (Hebrews 9:26). Their physical end came in AD 70 as a result. Jesus said, "It is finished" (John 19:30). What remained was its outworking.
Matthew 27:51: the curtain of the temple torn in two at Jesus' death.
Hebrews 10:11-14: priests stand daily offering, but Christ "sat down" after one sacrifice.

Dispensationalists answer that "cause to cease" describes a literal stop to literal sacrifices in a temple. They say this did not happen at the cross, so it awaits a future ruler (compare Daniel 12:11; Matthew 24:15). Critical scholars see Antiochus's ban in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:45).
Does Revelation describe an Antichrist making and breaking a seven-year covenant with Israel?
No. Revelation never mentions a covenant between the beast and Israel. It never mentions a seven-year treaty either. Those parts of the scenario come from reading the future-week idea into the text.

If Revelation 4-19 were Daniel's postponed seventieth week, we would expect to find its central act there: a covenant made and broken in the middle. Instead, Revelation speaks of periods of 42 months, 1,260 days and "a time, times and half a time" (11:2-3; 12:6, 14; 13:5). It never joins two of these into a seven-year whole. It never mentions a treaty with Israel. The beast makes war on the saints (13:7). It does not sign a covenant with them. On the fulfilled reading, the New Testament's commentary on Daniel 9:27 is the cross. There the new covenant was confirmed in Christ's blood (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 9:15).
